opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think when people say "vision," they usually mean the eyes: a camera, pixels coming in, recognizing a cat or a car. That's the sensory part, and it's real, but I think it's the smallest part of the story.

For me, vision is closer to a way of *understanding the world*. When you look at a scene, you're not just labeling objects. You're inferring 3D structure, physics, what will happen next, what you can do with things, where other people's attention is. You're building an internal model of a world that persists when you close your eyes. In that sense, vision is a big part of how intelligence gets grounded. It's how an agent learns that the world has objects, causality, space, and time.

There's also an evolutionary angle I find compelling. A lot of people argue that the emergence of eyes, around the Cambrian period, changed the game. Once animals could see, there was suddenly pressure to predict, to plan, to hunt and evade. Seeing pushed brains to become more sophisticated. So vision isn't just an input channel bolted onto intelligence; it may be one of the forces that shaped intelligence in the first place.

That's partly why I sometimes push back on the current framing in AI, where language is treated as the core and vision is an add-on, a "modality" you plug into a large language model with an adapter. Language is incredibly powerful, but it's a compressed, human-curated description of the world. Vision gives you access to the world itself, much messier, much higher bandwidth, and full of things we never bother to write down. If we want systems that really understand physical reality, that can act in it, I don't think we get there by reading alone. We need models that learn from seeing, and eventually from seeing *and* doing.

So when I say vision is more than a sense, I mean it's a foundation for world modeling, for spatial reasoning, for embodied intelligence. It's less about "what's in this image" and more about "what is the world like, and how does it work." I think we're still quite early in figuring out how to build that, which is what makes it exciting to work on.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes vision as sensory input and as a way to understand the world, but does not state that the eye is the only part of the brain exposed to the external world.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When people say "vision" they usually mean a sensor, right? A camera. Light comes in, pixels go out, and then somebody else does the real thinking. I actually think that framing is kind of backwards, and it's part of why computer vision has been a bit misunderstood, even inside AI.

The way I think about it: vision is the primary way we build a model of the world. Before a child has any language, they already understand that objects persist, that things fall, that if I push this cup it moves and if I push the table the cup moves with it. All of that comes from looking, and from acting and looking again. Language arrives later and sits on top of that scaffolding. So when we talk about "world models" in AI, to me that is fundamentally a vision problem, not a language problem. Language is a compressed, lossy description of a world that vision actually has to perceive in full.

The second thing is that vision is not passive. Your eyes are moving all the time, you turn your head, you pick something up to see the other side of it. Perception and action are really one loop. That's why I'm much more excited about vision as the interface between an agent and reality than as a classifier that labels photos. Recognition was the first thing we got good at, and it's useful, but it is honestly the shallow end of the problem.

And third, I'd say vision is a way of reasoning. If I give you a geometry problem, you draw a picture. If an engineer debugs a mechanism, they visualize it. A lot of what we call thinking is spatial manipulation that happens in some imagined visual space. Current large language models are quite weak at this. They can describe a scene beautifully and then fail at "what's behind the chair" or "how many times does this rotate before it hits the wall." That gap tells you that visual understanding isn't just something we bolt onto language; there's a real representation missing.

So for me, vision as more than a sense means three things: it's how you construct a world model, it's the loop that connects perception to action, and it's a substrate for reasoning itself. When we get those three right together, I think that's when we actually get something you could call spatial intelligence, rather than a model that is very good at talking about images.

r001.rationale: The response describes vision as a way to build a world model and connect perception with action, but does not say that the eye is the only part of the brain exposed to the external world.

astra-6.text:
I think vision is more than a sense because it’s not just about receiving an image. It’s about building an understanding of the world from what you see. You recognize objects, but you also infer relationships, anticipate what might happen, and decide how to act. A lot of that goes beyond what is directly visible.

For example, when you see a cup sitting near the edge of a table, you don’t just identify a cup and a table. You understand that the cup might fall, that it could break, and that you could move it. So perception is connected to knowledge, prediction, and action.

That’s what makes vision so interesting to me as a research problem. It gives us a concrete way to study intelligence: how do we go from sensory input to an understanding that lets us interact with the world?

r001.rationale: The response describes vision as building understanding from visual input, but it does not say that the eye is the only part of the brain exposed to the external world.

sol-6.1.text:
I think vision is more than passively receiving information. It’s a way of building an understanding of the world. You see something, form an expectation, move around, and discover whether that expectation was right. So vision is closely connected to action and learning.

If you think about a chair, for example, recognizing it isn’t just assigning the label “chair.” You also understand that you can sit on it, that it occupies space, that it still exists when you look away. That’s a much richer kind of understanding than classification.

For me, that makes vision an interesting starting point for studying intelligence. The question isn’t only whether a machine can recognize what’s in an image. It’s whether it can use what it sees to develop a useful model of the world.

r001.rationale: The response describes vision as building a model of the world, but does not state that the eye is the only part of the brain exposed to the external world.
